facts.value: The control unit manages the computer's various components; it reads and interprets the program instructions, transforming them into control signals that activate other parts of the computer.
A key component common to all CPUs is the program counter, a special memory cell that keeps track of which location in memory the next instruction is to be read from.

The control system reads the code for the next instruction, decodes it into commands for other systems, increments the program counter, reads required data, provides necessary data to an ALU or register, instructs hardware to perform operations, and writes results back to memory or output devices.
The program counter can be changed by calculations done in the ALU; adding 100 to the program counter causes the next instruction to be read from a location 100 further down.
Instructions that modify the program counter are known as 'jumps' and allow for loops and conditional instruction execution.
The sequence of operations that the control unit goes through to process an instruction is akin to a short computer program.
In some complex CPU designs, there is another smaller computer called a microsequencer, which runs a microcode program that causes events to happen.
The control unit, ALU, and registers are collectively known as a central processing unit (CPU).
Since the 1970s, CPUs have typically been constructed on a single MOS integrated circuit chip called a microprocessor.
